t.1.38.2: May good fortune be yours! I wish to hear this story in full, O Brahman: how did my ancestor carry out the sacrifice?
t.1.38.1: Having heard Viśvāmitra's words at the end of the tale, O Raghunandana, he spoke, supremely delighted, to the sage who shone like a blazing fire.
t.1.38.3: Then Viśvāmitra, as if smiling, said to Kākutstha: "Rāma, let the full account of the great-souled Sagara be heard."
t.1.38.4: Himavān, the foremost of mountains, known as the father-in-law of Śaṃkara, faces the Vindhya mountain, and the two gaze at one another.
t.1.38.6: O Kākutstha, dear one, the great chariot-warrior Aṃśumān of the firm bow, abiding by the will of Sagara, conducted the wandering of his horse.
t.1.38.5: Between those two that sacrifice was begun, O best of men, for that region, O tiger among men, is renowned as fit for the performance of sacrifice.
t.1.38.7: While he was performing that sacrifice, at its appointed juncture Vāsava took on the body of a rākṣasa and carried off the sacrificial horse.
t.1.38.8: But, O Kākutstha, as the horse of that great-souled one was being carried off, all the assembled priests then spoke to the sacrificer.
t.1.38.9: This sacrificial horse is being swiftly carried off during the sacred rite. Slay the thief, O Kākutstha, and let the horse be brought back.
t.1.38.10: This is a breach in the sacrifice, and it bodes ill for all of us. Therefore, O king, let that be done by which the rite may be made whole and free of any flaw.
t.1.38.11: Having heard the words of his preceptor in that assembly, the king spoke these words to his sixty thousand sons.
t.1.38.12: O sons, bulls among men, I see no way in for the rākṣasas, for this great sacrifice has been undertaken by illustrious ones purified by mantras.
t.1.38.14: O sons, each of you go forth over an expanse of one yojana, and dig up the earth until the horse is found.
t.1.38.13: So go, my dear sons, and search for it; may good fortune be with you. Range over the whole earth, garlanded by the ocean.
t.1.38.15: Go forth at my command and search for that very thief of the horse, for I, consecrated for the sacrifice, must remain here together with my grandson and the company of preceptors.
t.1.38.16: "I shall stay here until the horse is seen; good fortune to you!" When this had been said, the mighty princes were glad at heart.
t.1.38.17: O Rāma, bound by their father's command, they went forth over the surface of the earth, each one taking for himself a stretch of ground a yojana in extent.
t.1.38.18: O tiger among men, they split open the earth with arms whose touch was like the thunderbolt, with spears like lightning, and with exceedingly dreadful ploughs.
t.1.38.19: As it was being split open, O Raghunandana, the earth cried out, and so did the Nāgas and Asuras who were being slain, O Rāghava.
t.1.38.20: O Raghunandana, a dreadful cry arose from the rākṣasas and other creatures, spreading across sixty thousand yojanas.
t.1.38.21: Thus the heroic sons of the king split open the earth, Jambūdvīpa crowded with mountains, down to the unsurpassed Rasātala.
t.1.38.22: Digging, O tiger among kings, they went about on every side. Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, the Asuras and the serpents...
t.1.38.24: Utterly terrified, they spoke these words to the Grandsire: "O Blessed One, the whole earth is being dug up by the sons of Sagara."
t.1.38.23: Then all of them, their minds deeply troubled, approached the Grandfather, and with downcast faces they sought to win the favor of that great-souled one.
t.1.38.25: And many great-souled creatures dwelling in the waters are being slain, as they cry, “This one is the destroyer of our sacrifice; by him the horse is being carried off.”
t.1.38.26: Thus those sons of Sagara are slaying all beings.
